## The story

Global payments platform Paysafe has engaged Altimetrik, an artificial intelligence engineering firm, to modernize and scale its technology infrastructure. The partnership, announced in a press release dated Wednesday, November 18, covers Paysafe’s platforms and product engineering, data and AI foundations, and AI-led agentic operations. Altimetrik will also collaborate on improving system reliability during peak payment periods, as well as on Salesforce engineering and user experience engineering. Paysafe Chief Product Officer Bob Legters said the company sought a specialist partner that works directly with product teams and is accountable for business results, adding that Altimetrik’s AI capability will help Paysafe move faster while allowing its engineers to focus on the product roadmap. Altimetrik Chief Revenue Officer Gautam Samanta noted that the firm’s teams have built and modernized payments systems for banks and fintech leaders worldwide, giving them experience with the regulatory and uptime demands of such platforms.

## Key details

The engagement spans multiple layers of Paysafe’s technology stack. According to the release, Altimetrik will help strengthen Paysafe’s data and machine learning foundation and implement AI across engineering and day-to-day operations. The scope includes platform and product engineering, data and AI, and what the companies describe as AI-led agentic operations. System reliability during peak payment periods is a specific focus area, alongside Salesforce engineering and user experience engineering. Paysafe’s platform serves the experience economy, connecting businesses, consumers, and fans across gaming, iGaming, video gaming, esports, events, travel, hospitality, online trading, and digital commerce. The partnership follows two recent Paysafe product announcements. On Tuesday, November 17, Paysafe launched PaysafeGo, a solution designed to let enterprises launch branded digital wallets while avoiding the operational and regulatory complexity of being a wallet operator. Legters said at the time that consumers increasingly expect seamless experiences and payments are a critical part of that journey. On October 28, Paysafe announced that PaysafeWallet, accessible through the PaysafeCard app, had become available in all euro area markets, combining cash and digital money management in a single experience.

## Why it matters

The agreement illustrates how established payment processors are turning to specialist AI engineering firms to accelerate the modernization of legacy processing architectures. Paysafe’s platform must maintain high availability and regulatory compliance across a diverse set of verticals, each with distinct peak-load patterns and risk profiles. By outsourcing elements of AI integration, data foundation work, and reliability engineering to a partner with documented experience in banking and fintech systems, Paysafe aims to reduce the time its internal engineers spend on infrastructure and increase focus on product differentiation. The emphasis on agentic operations suggests a move toward autonomous monitoring, incident response, and optimization workflows that can operate continuously without human operators in the loop for routine tasks. This aligns with a broader industry trend where payment networks invest in AI-driven observability and self-healing capabilities to meet tightening uptime expectations from merchants and regulators. The concurrent launch of PaysafeGo and the expansion of PaysafeWallet indicate that Paysafe is simultaneously pursuing a platform strategy — enabling other businesses to embed wallet functionality — and a direct-to-consumer wallet play in Europe. Both initiatives increase transaction volume and data diversity on the core platform, reinforcing the need for a scalable, AI-enhanced operational backbone. For Altimetrik, the deal represents a reference engagement in the payments sector that can be cited when pursuing similar modernization mandates at other financial institutions. The partnership also highlights the growing role of Salesforce and user experience engineering in payments, as firms seek to unify customer-facing workflows across acquisition, onboarding, and support. Overall, the collaboration signals that AI adoption in payments is shifting from experimental pilots to embedded, cross-functional programs that touch core processing, data infrastructure, and customer experience simultaneously.

rising.longSummary:
## The story
Academic researchers from the University of Massachusetts have identified security weaknesses in the United States Automated Clearing House (ACH) network, according to a Payments Dive report published in 2024. The study was conducted as part of broader academic efforts to assess the resilience of critical financial infrastructure and was presented at a relevant research forum. Payments Dive covered the findings, noting that the researchers focused on protocol-level vulnerabilities rather than demonstrating a live attack in the wild. The report describes how certain existing ACH message-handling procedures contain conditions under which malformed or unexpected inputs could be processed, potentially creating unintended transaction paths. The University of Massachusetts team responsibly disclosed their findings to industry stakeholders, though the article does not specify immediate remediation timelines. The coverage emphasizes that the work is exploratory in nature, aiming to surface design assumptions that have persisted in the ACH system for decades. By bringing these assumptions into focus, the research seeks to inform future updates to operating rules and validation frameworks.

## Key details
The research, as detailed by Payments Dive, targets the core operating rules and message formats that govern how financial institutions originate, route, and settle ACH transactions. Specific weaknesses relate to insufficient verification steps in certain transaction pathways, particularly where legacy routing logic intersects with modern clearing expectations. The study outlines how these misalignment points could be exploited if an actor were able to submit carefully crafted messages that bypass standard validation checks. Payments Dive reported that the researchers identified multiple such vectors, though the article refrains from listing technical specifics beyond what is necessary to illustrate the concept. The UMass team’s analysis also considers how the ACH network’s reliance on batch processing and standardized file formats may limit the speed with which security patches can be applied across the industry. The findings are situated within a broader academic trend of examining payment-system security, a field that has historically received less attention than consumer-facing fintech platforms. The article notes that the researchers did not name specific banks or processors affected, nor did they quantify the likelihood of real-world exploitation; instead, they provided a risk taxonomy intended to guide further analysis.

## Why it matters
The ACH network remains the backbone of U.S. electronic payments, handling direct deposits, payroll, Social Security benefits, and bill payments on a massive scale. The Federal Reserve reported in 2023 that ACH processed approximately $73 trillion in payments annually, a figure that underscores the system’s systemic importance. Even theoretical protocol weaknesses can have practical implications for clearing banks and originators that operate on the assumption that ACH messages conform to strict validation rules. If the described vectors were to be actively exploited, the potential consequences include disrupted payment timing, unauthorized routing of funds, and increased operational risk for institutions processing high volumes of recurring transactions. Payments Dive notes that the study has already prompted conversations among compliance and risk teams about the need for updated validation software and stronger inter-institution communication regarding protocol changes. The research also highlights a growing recognition that the ACH architecture, largely unchanged in its foundational rules since the 1970s, may require systematic security reviews as the industry modernizes to support faster and real-time payment capabilities. For the product team, the key takeaway is that protocol-level risks in core payment infrastructure can have system-wide ripple effects, warranting closer coordination between technology, risk, and compliance functions to ensure that new features or system updates do not inadvertently reintroduce or overlook foundational vulnerabilities.

africa.longSummary:
## The story

Moniepoint Microfinance Bank has commissioned its North Central regional headquarters in Abuja, according to a TechCabal report by Progress Godfrey dated November 21, 2026. The opening was reported as part of the bank’s physical expansion. It comes as the Central Bank of Nigeria requires nationally licensed microfinance banks to establish physical locations alongside their digital operations.

The article says the move reflects a broader regulatory push for fintechs to respond to growing customer bases and operations with increased physical presence. By requiring a stronger physical footprint, regulators want to ensure that nationwide digital banking operations are matched by accessible, in-person customer support.

At the commissioning on Friday, Babatunde Olofin, Moniepoint MFB’s managing director, said the bank plans to replicate the regional headquarters model in other parts of the country. The bank processes more than ₦1 trillion ($719.8 million) daily for 21 million customers, according to Olofin. The Abuja office is part of a wider physical network that already includes offices and service centres in northern states such as Borno, Bauchi, Kaduna, Kano and Sokoto. Moniepoint also operates a nationwide point-of-sale network serving businesses across all 774 local government areas.

The expansion comes as digital payments gain ground among businesses in northern Nigeria, where cash has traditionally dominated commercial activity. In Borno State, for instance, more than 45% of customers in some markets prefer digital payments. Bank transfers accounted for 28.6% and POS payments 17%. Olofin said physical locations would help the bank serve customers who may be less comfortable resolving banking issues through digital channels alone.

## Key details

The CBN requirement is central. Moniepoint said it opened the Abuja facility to meet the microfinance licensing physical presence requirements. The bank’s managing director said the plan is not to adopt the expensive, branch-heavy model of traditional commercial banks. Instead, it will maintain minimal physical hubs where customers can access relationship managers and resolve complex issues.

Olofin said the leaner approach limits expansion costs, while maintaining physical locations and staffing them will still increase the fintech’s operating expenses. He said the bank started in informal sectors that traditional bankers did not serve, including people selling spare parts in Ladipo and women selling corn on the streets. He said many of these people are not technically educated and that there should be a place where people can easily walk in, get served in any local language of their choice, and ensure that their money is safe. He also said, “Banking is a business of trust.”

Nigeria’s Vice President Kashim Shettima, represented by the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, linked the expansion to the broader push to deepen financial inclusion and support small businesses. Shettima said technology offers speed and reach, but people also need someone who can explain. He said Moniepoint’s decision to combine digital services with face-to-face assistance responds to an important reality.

Beyond physical expansion, the article says Moniepoint is deepening its lending business after disbursing over ₦1 trillion ($719.8 million) in loans to small businesses in 2025. The company plans to expand credit access further to micro-businesses, agriculture and Compressed Natural Gas initiatives. Chief Business Officer Tobi Amira said businesses that access Moniepoint’s working capital loans see an average 40% year-on-year growth in transaction volume.

## Why it matters

The story suggests that Nigerian fintechs are moving from digital-only scaling toward regulated physical footprints. For a bank product team member, the practical question is how licensing, compliance and customer support models interact with digital-first products. Moniepoint’s approach appears to combine digital infrastructure with minimal physical hubs rather than traditional branches.

The broader implication is that fintechs taking on regulated financial institution obligations may need physical infrastructure even when their initial model relied on agents or digital channels. The article notes that in June, TechCabal reported that Kuda Microfinance Bank plans to open more experience centres for customer support and community engagement after receiving a national microfinance bank licence from the CBN.

Moniepoint also says it has grown from TeamApt into one of Nigeria’s largest payment and business banking platforms and says it has created over one million jobs through its agency banking and merchant network. Its growing physical footprint reflects a broader shift in Nigeria’s fintech industry, where companies that initially scaled through digital platforms and agent networks are increasingly investing in physical infrastructure as they take on the obligations of regulated financial institutions.

For a product team, the note points to a continuing tension between digital scale and physical trust. The article presents the Abuja headquarters as a compliance-driven step, but also as a way to support customers who may prefer face-to-face help. That distinction could matter for how banks design support channels, agent networks and branch-light service models. The article does not estimate the cost of the new headquarters or its staffing beyond saying operating expenses will increase.

africa.longSummary:
## The story

LemFi, the diaspora-focused fintech founded in 2021 by Ridwan Olalere and Rian Cochran, is expanding well beyond its roots in cross-border remittances. The company, which reports more than two million customers—predominantly migrants and diaspora communities moving money across Africa, Asia, and Europe—is rolling out consumer credit, savings, and eSIM mobile-data services in a significant product push. The new offerings are initially available in the UK, with rollout to other markets planned subsequently. LemFi’s rebrand and app rebuild accompany the launch, designed to signal this strategic shift to investors, partners, and users alike. In a statement reflecting the company’s philosophy, co-founder and chief executive Ridwan Olalere said the existing financial system treats customers “as if they can only exist in one place at a time,” adding that this is “the wrong answer for people this ambitious.” The expansion positions LemFi not merely as a transfer platform but as a full-fledged consumer financial services provider for people whose lives span multiple countries.

## Key details

The most structurally significant addition is LemFi’s credit product, a revolving credit line issued through Pillar, an FCA-regulated credit provider the company acquired in 2025. The facility appears as a virtual card compatible with Apple Pay and Google Pay and can be used for both everyday spending and international transfers. Eligible customers can also view their Equifax credit score within the app at no cost, a feature LemFi is positioning as a direct response to the problem of credit histories failing to survive border crossings. The savings product is an instant-access account with a minimum opening deposit of £1, offering a boosted 5% AER for the first six months before reverting to a 3.04% AER tracker linked to the Bank of England base rate. Deposits are held by ClearBank and protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme up to £120,000 per eligible depositor, providing a structural backstop for the product. Complementing these financial tools, LemFi’s eSIM offering covers more than 100 destinations, allowing customers to purchase mobile data before arriving in a new country and thereby removing reliance on local SIM cards or roaming charges. All three products are launching first in the UK, with expansion to other markets on the company’s roadmap.

## Why it matters

LemFi’s move into regulated credit and savings represents a notable shift for a company traditionally anchored in remittances, reflecting a broader strategic pattern among cross-border neobanks that use transfer services as a customer-acquisition channel before layering higher-margin, regulated financial products on top. The global remittance market, estimated at roughly $905 billion in annual flows, has attracted a wave of specialist platforms including Wise, Remitly, Sendwave, and Nala, but most remain focused on the transfer product itself. By acquiring Pillar, LemFi secured a pre-existing FCA permission set, which shortens its licensing timeline; however, the company still faces capital-adequacy and conduct obligations associated with consumer credit. The firm has raised more than $85 million from investors including Highland Europe, Left Lane Capital, Palm Drive Capital, Endeavor Catalyst, and Y Combinator, providing a capital runway for this expansion. The eSIM product’s role—whether it generates meaningful incremental revenue or primarily serves as a retention and acquisition tool—remains to be seen, as does the performance of the Pillar-issued credit book as it scales across more than 30 corridors. Key milestones to watch include the rollout of credit and savings beyond the UK, the company’s ability to execute compliance requirements alongside payments infrastructure, and the eSIM product’s financial impact.

africa.longSummary:
## The story
Mukuru, a cross-border remittance platform, has expanded its pay-in network through a partnership with Flash, a payments technology company operating across Southern Africa. The collaboration integrates Mukuru’s cash settlement services into Flash’s merchant network, specifically placing pay-in points within spaza shops and other traditional trade outlets. This shift allows customers who previously needed to travel to banks or dedicated payment centers to complete transactions at locations near their homes, workplaces, or regular shopping routes. For individuals in townships, peri-urban neighborhoods, and rural areas—many of whom rely on cash and have had limited access to formal financial services, including South Africa’s migrant communities—the change removes a practical barrier and facilitates more timely remittances. Mukuru’s Commercial Manager for Cross-Border Remittances, Erone Kyte, noted that each additional pay-in point reduces an obstacle for customers sending money home. The partnership leverages Flash’s existing retail footprint to bring Mukuru’s services into everyday community spaces, with customers able to locate participating points via the Mukuru app or website. By situating pay-in points in shops people already visit, the companies aim to eliminate extra trips and make the payment process more efficient for senders who previously faced long distances to formal outlets. The integration represents a direct response to the challenges of cash-dependent cross-border sending in regions where bank branches and dedicated payment kiosks are sparse and often unreachable for low-income populations.

## Key details
The integration adds cash pay-in capabilities across Flash’s broad merchant footprint, which encompasses spaza shops and other traditional trade outlets that serve a significant share of South African consumers. Data tracked by Trade Intelligence places the informal payments sector at approximately R750 billion, with recent total turnover reaching R197 billion and growing at roughly 15 percent annually. Research confirms that traditional trade and spaza shops are expanding faster than large supermarket chains, with almost 80 percent of South African households shopping at these outlets regularly. By positioning Mukuru services within this high-traffic retail channel, the partnership taps into a distribution network that reaches urban, township, and rural populations where formal banking infrastructure is sparse. Mukuru and Flash intend to raise awareness of the new pay-in option through store signage, digital campaigns, and community promotions in the coming months. The companies note that this effort is part of Mukuru’s ongoing initiative over the past two years to enlarge its pay-in network and improve access to remittance services across the region. Customers can identify their nearest participating Flash pay-in point using the Mukuru app or website. The partnership also stands to benefit shop owners, who can draw additional foot traffic by offering remittance services alongside everyday goods, creating a mutually reinforcing relationship between financial inclusion and informal retail.

## Why it matters
The partnership addresses a persistent access gap for cash-dependent senders, particularly migrant communities in Southern Africa, who often face long travel distances to reach formal pay-in locations. By embedding remittance services within familiar neighborhood spaza shops, Mukuru and Flash seek to reduce the time and effort required for cross-border payments, making the process more convenient for both senders and recipients. The integration also benefits shop owners by diversifying the services they offer, potentially increasing foot traffic and community engagement. From a broader sector perspective, the move underscores the growing role of traditional trade outlets in financial inclusion, as they serve a large and expanding share of the population in underserved areas. The collaboration reflects an industry trend of leveraging existing retail infrastructure to extend financial services to populations with limited bank access. If the model proves effective, it could influence how remittance and payment providers partner with informal merchants to broaden reach and improve service convenience across the region, offering a replicable approach for extending financial tools to populations historically excluded from formal banking systems.

africa.longSummary:
## The story  
Benin’s Ministry of Digital Transformation and Innovation convened the AfriLabs 2026 Annual Gathering in Cotonou, a conference that gathered entrepreneurs, investors, policymakers and other stakeholders in Africa’s innovation ecosystem. The event’s theme, “Africa’s Innovation Era: Building Sustainable Institutions for Global Influence and Continental Impact,” emphasized the need for institutions, policies and partnerships that can ensure technology endures and reaches the people it is meant to serve. Minister Mahuna Akplogan framed the discussion around a simple test: can people actually use the technology? He noted that while Benin has launched more than 250 e‑services, many citizens remain excluded because the services are delivered only in French, a language spoken by roughly 34 % of the country’s nearly 14 million population. To bridge this gap, the ministry introduced “J’aime ma langue,” a project that aims to develop voice‑to‑voice AI models for indigenous languages such as Fon, Dendi, Bariba, Yoruba and English. The minister argued that digital tools must adapt to users rather than force users to adapt to technology, and that voice interfaces will allow people to interact with services by speaking rather than reading or writing in languages they do not normally use. The initiative is presented as both a technical effort and an expression of the value of local languages, with the ultimate goal of making public services usable for those previously excluded.

## Key details  
- The AfriLabs 2026 gathering took place at the Sofitel Cotonou Marina Hotel from 18 November 2026, hosted jointly by Benin’s Ministry of Digital Transformation and Innovation and AfriLabs, a pan‑African network supporting technology hubs.  
- Minister Mahuna Akplogan reported that Benin has deployed more than 250 e‑services, but accessibility is limited for those who do not speak French.  
- Linguistic data from the article indicates that about 34 % of Benin’s population speaks French, leaving the majority without a language that matches the current digital services.  
- “J’aime ma langue” seeks to create multilingual speech models that enable citizens to request services, such as police record inquiries, by speaking in Fon, Dendi, Bariba, Yoruba or English.  
- The project focuses on voice‑to‑voice interfaces; written material may be used for training, but the intended tools will let users speak rather than type.  
- Akplogan emphasized that technology development should be driven by local needs, stating that “it is up to us, Beninese and Africans, to invent the best way to use these technologies.”  
- The minister called for public institutions to become early adopters and catalysts for local innovation, rather than merely purchasing external solutions.  
- Benin aims to become a technology exporter, a goal shared by other smaller African nations such as Sierra Leone, which are leveraging digital governance and civic technology to shift from being tech consumers to regional innovation leaders.  
- The conference program covered policy, data and AI, investment, creative industries, makerspaces, trade, and the green and blue economy, underscoring that innovation spans multiple sectors and requires cross‑border collaboration.  
- Akplogan highlighted “innovation houses” as a mechanism for bringing together entrepreneurs, government, municipalities and public administrations to address real‑world problems collaboratively.

## Why it matters  
The initiative illustrates a shift from simply digitizing services to ensuring those services are linguistically and culturally accessible to the populations they intend to serve. By prioritizing voice interfaces in indigenous languages, Benin addresses both literacy barriers and the dominance of French in public digital interactions, potentially increasing participation among the 66 % of citizens who do not speak French. This approach aligns with broader continental goals of building sustainable institutions that can translate local knowledge into usable services, thereby fostering inclusive growth. Moreover, the emphasis on local ownership of technology development challenges the notion that external solutions automatically meet African community needs, encouraging home‑grown innovation that can be exported across the continent. If successful, the model could inform other public‑sector digital transformations in multilingual African contexts, demonstrating how adaptive, people‑first technology can enhance service delivery, reduce exclusion, and support long‑term institutional resilience.

ghana.longSummary:
## The story

Ghana's Rent Control Department plans to digitise its operations by the end of the first quarter of 2027, according to Acting Rent Control Commissioner Frederick Opoku. Speaking on JoyNews' *Newsfile* programme on Saturday, November 21, Mr Opoku presented the move as part of a broader internal reform effort intended to close administrative gaps and make the department's services more professional and accessible. The remarks were reported by Techfocus24.

The announcement bundles two separate changes. The first is digitisation of tenancy paperwork: landlords and prospective tenants would be able to go online, download tenancy agreement forms and complete them through what the commissioner described as a coded verification system. The second is a tightening of the department's gatekeeping. Landlords approaching the department would first have to register officially to establish that they are legitimate property owners, and tenants would have to produce rent cards as evidence of their tenancy before complaints are entertained.

Mr Opoku said these requirements are already provided for in existing law but have not been consistently enforced, and that this gap has created loopholes in the rental regulation system. The article does not say whether funding, procurement, a technology partner or any legislative amendment has been arranged, and it gives no technical detail on how the coded verification would operate or whether it would connect to national identity systems.

## Key details

- **Target date:** first three months of 2027. Mr Opoku described the plan as part of reforms introduced during his first year in office.
- **Online tenancy agreements:** forms would be downloadable and completed digitally. Beyond the reference to a "coded" verification step, the mechanism is unspecified in the reporting.
- **Landlord registration:** landlords would need to register to prove ownership or landlord status before their complaints are considered.
- **Tenant evidence:** rent cards would serve as proof of a tenancy arrangement.
- **Legal footing:** the commissioner says the requirements rest on existing statutes; the article does not name them. Ghana's rent regulation framework is generally associated with the Rent Act, 1962 (Act 220) and the Rent Control Law, 1986 (PNDCL 138), with the department sitting under the Ministry of Works and Housing.
- **Pilot numbers:** approximately 3,000 landlords were registered through a pilot at the department's Greater Accra office over the preceding three months, according to Mr Opoku. The article gives no indication of how many landlords the department ultimately aims to register nationally.
- **Context:** the announcement came amid public debate over accommodation costs at the University of Ghana, after University of Ghana Enterprises Limited proposed a 26 per cent hostel fee increase, which was later reduced following consultations with student leaders.

## Why it matters

The department's central weakness has long been records. A functioning register of landlords, combined with digitised tenancy agreements, would give it a searchable base for enforcement, dispute handling and analysis of rent levels — capabilities that a paper-based office handling walk-in complaints struggles to sustain. The Greater Accra pilot is a modest start, but it is the first concrete evidence in this reporting that registration is producing data rather than just procedures.

The verification requirements cut both ways. Requiring landlords to prove ownership before their complaints are heard could filter out spurious claims and give tenants a measure of protection against people who do not actually control the property. Requiring tenants to produce rent cards, however, assumes a formal written tenancy exists. Tenants in informal arrangements — sublets, family properties, verbal agreements — may find themselves unable to access the department's complaint process at all. The article does not address how those cases would be handled.

Digitisation also raises access questions. The plan as described is online-first, and the reporting does not say whether physical channels will remain available for people without reliable internet access, smartphones or the literacy to complete forms unaided. In a sector where the most vulnerable tenants are often the least connected, that design choice matters as much as the technology itself.

On implementation, the 2027 target is roughly a year out and no budget line, vendor, procurement route or delivery milestone has been disclosed. Public-sector IT rollouts in the region frequently slip past announced dates, and the absence of detail here makes the timeline difficult to assess. The gap between announcing a platform and operating one is where most such projects are won or lost.

Politically, rental affordability is live. The University of Ghana episode showed how quickly accommodation costs become a public issue, and a regulator with better data and a formal register would be better placed to intervene credibly — but it would also face sharper questions about how rents are set and enforced.

What to watch: whether new regulations or a legislative instrument accompany the enforcement changes; whether the platform integrates with national ID; whether the registration pilot extends beyond Accra; whether the 2027 budget estimates contain a corresponding allocation; and whether the department publishes any of the data it collects.

## The story

MTN Group Board Chairman Mcebisi Jonas and MTN Ghana CEO Stephen Blewett met with Ghana’s Minister of Finance, Hon. Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, according to Techfocus24. The meeting was described as a courtesy call and formed part of a series of high-level stakeholder engagements commemorating MTN Ghana’s 30th anniversary.

The article notes that over the past three decades, MTN Ghana had evolved from a telecommunications pioneer into a key enabler of national development. During the engagement, Jonas reaffirmed MTN’s long-term commitment to Ghana. He described Ghana as a key investment destination and an important market within the Group’s operations. He said MTN recognizes progress in strengthening the country’s economic foundations and appreciates its constructive relationship with government. The company’s stated focus is on translating that partnership into investment that improves connectivity, expands opportunity, and supports Ghana’s digital transformation.

The Minister welcomed the delegation and commended MTN for three decades of sustained investment in Ghana’s telecommunications and digital financial ecosystem. He noted that such partnerships remain vital to advancing sustainable economic growth and job creation. Jonas emphasized the importance of strong public-private collaboration in shaping the country’s digital future.

## Key details

The article identifies Mcebisi Jonas as MTN Group Board Chairman, Stephen Blewett as MTN Ghana CEO, and Hon. Dr Cassiel Ato Forson as Minister for Finance. The meeting took place on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, and was part of MTN Ghana’s 30th anniversary commemorations, marking three decades since the company introduced commercial GSM mobile telephony to Ghana in 1996.

According to the article, MTN’s contributions over the past 30 years include sustained capital investment, significant fiscal contributions, local equity participation on the Ghana Stock Exchange, and social interventions delivered through the MTN Ghana Foundation. The company says it remains committed to deepening investment, advancing digital and financial inclusion, and contributing to Ghana’s growth and development.

The article does not disclose specific funding amounts, capital expenditure figures, or timelines for new projects. Jonas said Ghana has been an important part of MTN’s story for three decades and that the company’s commitment to its future remains strong. He also characterized the relationship with government as constructive.

## Why it matters

For a bank product team, this development matters because mobile network infrastructure frequently serves as the backbone for mobile money and other digital financial services. A pledge by a major operator to maintain and expand connectivity in Ghana implies continued support for the digital rails used for payments, account access, and credit delivery, particularly in areas where traditional bank branches are limited. For banks, the reliability and reach of that infrastructure can affect onboarding costs, transaction volumes, and the feasibility of agent banking or digital wallet partnerships.

The engagement also illustrates how a multinational telecommunications firm manages sovereign relations after three decades in an emerging market. The combination of a local equity listing on the Ghana Stock Exchange, fiscal contributions, and a corporate social foundation shows one model for embedding a foreign operator within a national economy. For product teams outside banking, it offers a case study in how telecom providers evolve from voice services into enablers of digital financial ecosystems, and how anniversary milestones and ministerial meetings are used to signal stability to regulators, customers, and markets.

Readers should treat MTN’s investment pledge as a statement of intent rather than a committed capital plan, because the source text includes no specific amounts or implementation dates. The article frames the outlook as confidence in Ghana’s economic prospects, but it provides no granular financial details that would allow an assessment of scale or risk.

ghana.longSummary:
## The story

Ghana's National Petroleum Authority (NPA) has commissioned a research study with the Brew-Hammond Energy Centre at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) to model how electric vehicle adoption could affect the Authority's revenue. The work is titled *An Assessment of the Impact of Electric Vehicle Uptake on Revenues of the National Petroleum Authority, Ghana*, according to Techfocus24, which reported the partnership.

The study is designed to examine three linked questions: how much conventional fuel EV adoption might displace, what revenue that displacement could cost the NPA, and how the country's electric vehicle fleet is likely to grow over time. The stated purpose is to give the Authority an analytical basis for understanding how rising EV numbers could change petroleum consumption patterns and, in turn, the revenue framework of Ghana's downstream petroleum sector.

NPA Chief Executive Godwin Kudzo Tameklo Esq. met the research team as part of the engagement, and the Authority framed the meeting as a reaffirmation of its commitment to evidence-based policymaking and strategic planning. The article names the participants: Prof David Ato Quansah, Director of the Brew-Hammond Energy Centre; Dr Kwame Sarkodie, Head of the Department of Petroleum Engineering at KNUST; and Dr Joseph Wilson, Director of Research, Monitoring and Evaluation at the NPA.

The NPA said the partnership illustrates the value of collaboration between regulators and academic research centres on complex energy-sector problems, and described it as part of its broader commitment to research, innovation and credible data in regulatory decision-making.

## Key details

The scope described in the article is narrow and fiscal. The study is not presented as an assessment of EV policy, charging infrastructure or emissions. It is an exercise in revenue forecasting: projecting fleet growth, estimating fuel displacement, and translating both into expected changes in NPA revenue.

That framing matters because of how Ghana's downstream petroleum sector generates public money. Revenue is collected per litre of fuel sold, through a layered structure of levies and margins that typically includes earmarked funds for road maintenance, energy-sector purposes and price stabilization, alongside the Authority's own operational funding. A revenue model built on volume is therefore directly exposed to volume decline — even a slow one. The study appears intended to quantify that exposure rather than to argue for or against electrification.

The article does not disclose the study's timeline, cost, funding source, methodology, data sources or publication date. It also does not state whether the results will be made public or used internally for budget planning. Those gaps are worth noting: without a delivery date or a publication commitment, the practical value of the work to outside observers is hard to gauge.

The institutional pairing is notable in itself. The Brew-Hammond Energy Centre is one of Ghana's established energy research units at KNUST, and the Department of Petroleum Engineering sits within the same university — so the project draws on both energy-systems and petroleum expertise. On the government side, the presence of the NPA's director of research, monitoring and evaluation signals that the work is intended to feed into the Authority's own planning function rather than sit as an academic exercise.

## Why it matters

For a regulator whose funding is tied to fuel volumes, electrification is a slow-moving but structural issue. Two things make it worth tracking now rather than later. First, fiscal frameworks and levy structures are sticky: they are set in legislation, revised infrequently, and take time to redesign. If fuel displacement begins to erode the levy base, the options — adjusting rates, broadening the base to electricity or road use, or funding the regulator from general revenue — all require years of lead time. Modeling ahead of the problem is cheaper than reacting to it.

Second, there is a fairness question embedded in the numbers. If EVs use the same roads but do not contribute through fuel levies, the road-funding burden shifts toward remaining fuel users, who may be poorer or in commercial transport. That is a distributional issue as much as a revenue one, and it is the kind of question a modeling study can at least put numbers against.

The broader context the article cites is the global energy transition and the need for Ghana's downstream regulatory framework to respond to new technologies and shifting consumer preferences. That is a reasonable description of the pressure many petroleum regulators face, though the article gives no indication of how large Ghana's EV fleet currently is or how fast it is expected to grow — the central inputs to any such projection.

What to watch: whether the study is published, whether it produces a quantified revenue-loss range under different adoption scenarios, and whether the NPA follows it with any proposal to adjust its levy or funding structure. Any of those would turn a research announcement into a policy signal. Until then, this is a preparatory step — a regulator acknowledging that its revenue base and the country's transport fleet are no longer fixed assumptions.
